name: splunk-p1-getting-in
title: Splunk Case 01, Part 1: how the attacker got in

slides.kicker: case 01 · boss of the soc v1
slides.title: 412 passwords. One of them worked: batman.
slides.sub: How the attacker got into the website's admin page, traced in Splunk on the Boss of the SOC v1 practice dataset.

slides.title: Two IPs did most of the talking
bullets: 40.80.148[.]42: 17,483 requests from 21:36:45. Test strings marked `acunetix_wvs_security_test`: the Acunetix scanner.
23.22.63[.]114: 1,235 requests with User-Agent `Python-urllib/2.7`: a Python script.

slides.title: The script hit one page only
bullets: All 1,235 requests went to `/joomla/administrator/index.php`, the Joomla admin login.
823 GET and 412 POST: the login form was sent 412 times.
That is a brute force. It still doesn't tell me if a password worked.

slides.title: 412 POSTs, all for the user admin
slides.caption: 412 events, and every POST sends username=admin, each with a different password from a wordlist.

slides.title: Only one password was sent twice: batman.
body: Across all 14,238 POSTs, by both IPs. The query is on the cheat slide.
slides.caption: batman: count 2, from 23.22.63[.]114 and 40.80.148[.]42.

slides.title: The script found it. A browser used it 1 min 32 s later.
body: 21:46:33 the Python script, 21:48:05 Internet Explorer 11 from the scanner IP. Both got status 303, so 303 alone doesn't prove the login worked.
slides.caption: One attacker, two IPs, two tools.

slides.title: Cheat sheet: spot a web brute force in Splunk
bullets: Who talks most, and as what: `| stats count by src_ip, http_user_agent | sort - count`
What one IP hit: `src_ip=<ip> | stats count by http_method, uri_path`
A password sent twice: `http_method=POST | rex field=form_data "passwd=(?<password>[^&]+)" | stats count, values(src_ip) by password | where count > 1`
Status 303 is a redirect, not proof of a login. Check what the IP did next.
